catalog_quote: Accent: Like many other dialects of this group in this too the normal tendency of the speakers is to put heavier stress on the initial syllable of a word, but there are a few instances of monosyllabic words in which the stress, sometimes accompanied with a sort of high falling tone, becomes significant: /ná/ oath: /na/ bride, daughter-in-law, /lá/ cave: /la/ for, also; /ó/ breath: /o/ a kiss /sá/ vien: /sa/ grass. WORD STRUCTURE ... [p. 15] ... accent on the initial syllable. Consequently, the plosion as well as the voice/aspiration is reduced in every way, leading to their indeterminate perception, which may be described as- Devoicing: Voiced plosives /g, d, b/ ... [p. 21] ... accent (i.e., higher stress), quantity of the syllable peak or the patterns of the syllables concerned.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and normally falls on the first syllable of the word (strong enough that non-initial plosives are weakened/devoiced); separately, a handful of monosyllables are distinguished by a stressed/high-falling-tone vs. plain pronunciation (incipient tonal contrast), e.g. ná 'oath' vs na 'bride'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in the accessible text.
new_statements.exceptions: A few monosyllabic minimal pairs where stress accompanied by a high falling tone is 'significant' (ná/na, lá/la, ó/o, sá/sa); Sharma elsewhere (pp. 15-16, per Wikipedia's summary) associates high tone with vowels before word-final /h/ or after word-initial retroflex/dental plosives.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement ('initial syllable of a word') in the phonology part of the sketch; impressionistic fieldwork description, citation forms. Text recovered only from three overlapping Google Books search-within snippets of p. 18 (reassembled verbatim; the page scan itself was not served by automated download), so surrounding context (section numbering, any further sentences on polysyllables) is unseen.
new_statements.identity_note: Sharma's 'Jad dialect' = the Tibetic speech of the Jads of Nelang and Jadhang (Uttarkashi), now resident at Bagori (Harsil) and Dunda; language-level jadd1243. Glottolog splits Jad into Jadthang [jadd1242] and Nilang [nila1245]; the accessible snippets do not say which village(s) Sharma's consultants came from. Not to be confused with the 'Jad' community of Himachal Pradesh or with Rongpo/Marchha (the Jads also call themselves Rongpa).

tone_statements.citation: Tournadre, Nicolas & Hiroyuki Suzuki. 2023. The Tibetic Languages: an introduction to the family of languages derived from Old Tibetan (LACITO-Publications, Linguistic Diversity 2). Villejuif: LACITO-Publications (CNRS). 1151 pp., 17 maps. ISBN 978-2-490768-08-0. Part 2, chap. 9 'Inner classification of the Tibetic languages', sect. 9.9 'The Western section': Jadang (Dzad, Jad) pp. 593-594, 601; 9.9.6 'Phonological characteristics of the W section' pp. 603-604.
tone_statements.quote: The dialects of the Western section, including the two Jangthang dialects spoken in the state of Jammu Kashmir have a pitch tone system generally with a two-way contrast (high and low). This is a major distinction with the neighoring dialects of Ladakh (except the Jangthang dialects) and Zangskar. Concerning Pangi and Paldar, additional research is needed. [p. 603] ... Jadang dialect also called Dzad or Jad is spoken in Jadang and Nilang villages in Harsil Tehsil of Uttarkashi district (Uttarakhand). ... There is no recent data about the situation of the Jadang dialect. Grierson (1909) states that Jad is closely related to Spiti dialect. So far no linguistic data are available on Jadang and thus fieldwork is needed to establish the proximity between this language and the Spiti-Garsha-Khunu group of dialects. [p. 601]
